utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sakic.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, we stopped at the part of the first day, towards the end of the day. Could you please tell us, since there were problems with the map, could you tell us the first time that you saw Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic with their family --

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- could you tell us in which direction did they go and which direction did they come from?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Should I indicate that on the map?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Just describe it, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, this map, in relation to the terrain where I live, it's the other way around. So I said that they were going towards the shelter of Jozo Vrebac, but I actually showed with my hand that they were going in the direction of their houses. Well, it's logical if I said that they were going with their families in the shelter, that they were going there and not the way I indicated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you saw them coming from which direction with their families?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From their houses, past my house in the direction of the shelter at Jozo Vrebac's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What road leads from their house? Where does it lead to?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Should I indicate it -- no. That road leads from their house, it's a footpath, and leads to my house. Then there is a kind of widening so that you can go by car, and it goes in the direction of the house of Jozo Vrebac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they were going along that footpath --

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. When they were walking along that footpath --

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- you saw them coming from the direction of their houses?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that they came from the direction of their houses. They came up to my house, and then they went in the direction of the shelter with their family, the shelter of Jozo Vrebac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a road there that leads from the warehouse of Vlatko Kupreskic towards your house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there is. It's a footpath. You can't go any other way because that's the configuration of the terrain, that it's only a footpath up to my house. Then from my house, there is a wider, normal road that goes further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there are two paths?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So they were coming from their houses and not from the warehouse of Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, they came from my house, and they were going in the direction of the shelter of Jozo Vrebac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean from their house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, from my house towards the shelter of Jozo Vrebac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The army that you saw that was coming, which direction did they come from?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers that I saw came from the direction of Zume towards my house. They passed by my house on the upper side, next to the garage, and they went in the direction of the warehouse of Vlatko Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Mirjan and Zoran came back, you said you saw them coming back from Zume.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them coming back from Zume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they stay?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They stayed at my house. That means that they settled their families in the shelter, and they came back to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did Zoran Kupreskic go back once more?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He went back -- he was taking two women from the Didak family, refugees, Manda and Marica, and their children. I don't remember the children's names. He took them in the direction of Zume as well, to the shelter of Jozo Vrebac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, could you tell how many times you saw Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic on that day? Was it once, several times?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean the 16th?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the 16th, the first day of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw them four or five times, maybe more, but I'm sure of that much because my son was with them so I paid attention. I was concerned about them, where they were. They came to my house. In the course of the day, I saw them four or five times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go anywhere from the shelter on that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On that day, at about 5.00 or 6.00 p.m., we moved from that shelter to the shelter in the house of Niko Vidovic where they said it was safer, and we assumed it was safer. So that's where we moved. We found a lot of people there, men, women, and children, in the shelter where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is this shelter in Niko Vidovic's house, approximately in which part?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's in the direction of Zume, from my house towards the shelter of Jozo Vrebac, but it's closer to my house than the shelter of Jozo Vrebac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's in the same direction, so it's in the area of Santici?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's on the border of Santici and Pirici. I think even that the house belongs more to Pirici than Santici, the house of Niko Vidovic where we moved to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at these photographs so you can tell us whose house is depicted?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would the usher please show the witness the photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D104/2.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Can I proceed? Well, this is the house of Niko Vidovic where the shelter was (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see all the other photographs?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I see this house. This is his house (indicating), and there's the road on one side which leads towards my house. It's on the left side. In relation to us, this is the entrance from the north side. This is the section of the shelter where we were, in the basement. This is the entrance to the basement, under these beams.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Would the usher please put the photographs on the ELMO so that we could see them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, was it a large house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was a large house. As you can see on the photograph, it's large. The basement is also large, but it wasn't appropriate. There was a lot of dampness there. It wasn't well insulated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the house on photograph number 1 is the house of Niko Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can put photographs 2 and 3 on the ELMO so that we can see the size of the basement.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is also the house. Yes, you want to see the inside of the basement. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the path; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That's the entrance to the basement from the upper side. Well, we still can't see the inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is photograph number 3. Photograph number 4?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This is the entrance to the basement, photograph number 4.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Photograph number 5?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this is a part of the basement. It was partitioned, I think, into two parts, but it was very unsuitable. There was no proper floor. There was no electricity or water. So there were no conditions really there for living. Not only for living, but even to stay for longer than eight hours, you really couldn't stay there for long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we look at photograph number 6?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, number 6.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 7? This is the interior of the basement. Could you tell us what the size of that basement was, and how many people were there in the basement?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you exactly, but maybe it was about 40 or 50 square metres. That was the size of it. I don't know exactly how many people there were, but basically nobody could lie down except for the children. No one could lie down except for the children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you see in the shelter? Did you see both Croats and Muslims, and who were they?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were both Muslims and Croats in the basement. From the Muslims, there were three families: Ramo Bilic, his wife and his three sons, his small sons at that time; Zijad, the brother of Ramo Bilic, his wife, and his two small sons; their brother-in-law, Miralem Strmonja, with his pregnant wife and one or two children. I don't remember exactly. I think there was one, a little girl. We were all there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left on the first day to the shelter, to the shelter of Niko Vidovic, on that first day, did everybody who was in your house go?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we all went to that shelter from my basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you to go there or did you go by yourselves, on your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, nobody told us to go. We just spontaneously went. We were thinking that if there were more of us, we would be safer. That's what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you afraid that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Was I afraid? I will just tell you one thing: My grandson Bruno, I was holding him in my arms, and I asked my daughter-in-law, "Where is he?" That's how afraid I was. I don't know if you can be more afraid than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were you afraid of? What were you afraid of?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what I was afraid of, but I was scared of the gunfire and everything that was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Muslims who were in the shelter with you also afraid, in the shelter of Niko Vidovic, the Bilic and the Strmonja families?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were not afraid of us, the neighbours, but they were afraid just because of the gunfire. I don't think that they would have been there if they had been afraid of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you think that they were not afraid of their neighbours?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, because Ramo, as soon as the war stopped, called me on the telephone, and I talked to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your son Mirko Sakic come to see you in the shelter and to see his family, his wife and children?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Mirko came and Zoran Kupreskic came with him, they came together, saw us, how we were doing, and then they returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they know that the Ramic and the Strmonja families were in that shelter?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they did. From my house, from Mirko's apartment on the first floor, Mirko came and Zoran came, and they called some woman called Ranka, who used to work in UNPROFOR with Mirko, to take out the Bilic and Strmonja families, to get them out of there. I don't know if they succeeded in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told them to call UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because they could see them there -- I don't know who told them. I talked to them, and I said it would be good to get those families out of there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the second day, you were in that shelter. You saw your son, Mirko Sakic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them once or several times?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I saw them several times because they would come to eat something, to the house, and then I would also see them because I would go to the depression where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we're now talking about the second day when you were in the shelter of Niko Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them; they came. When I went home to feed my livestock, I would see them there in the depression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I saw five or six men there in that depression, and Mirjan was with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the evening on the second day, did anything happen when you were already in the shelter of Niko Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the second day, between 20.00 and 21.00 in the evening, there was some information which arrived. They said that the Mujahedeen had broken through the line and that we had to flee from there, so we set out in the direction of Rovna and Radak's Bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you remain?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the road, the people from the Vrebac shelter and the shelter we had been in met, so there were a lot of people there. We all set off in the direction of Rovna, and when we passed Radak's Bridge, people went into the houses. I went into the last house, and Nermin Strmonja and his wife and children were with me. We spent the night in the house of Slavko Santic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the house of Slavko Santic, Nermin Strmonja was there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the brother of Miralem who was with us in the first shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Nermin Strmonja is a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he's a Muslim. I still see him from time to time. We say hello. We have a chat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he go on from there or did anything bad happen to him then? Did he leave Rovna?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We spent the night at that house, and nothing bad happened to us there, either to him or to us. We were all there under the same conditions. The following morning, he went to Vranjska with his family where the majority population is Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you and the people who were there didn't do anything bad to him?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, everybody knows that, and thank God everyone is alive and well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of the person whose house it was in which you sheltered in Rovna?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The house of Slavko Santic, also known as Radak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He's a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you come back from Rovna?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I came back from Rovna, where I had spent the night, at 4.00 in the morning to feed my livestock and to see about my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you come back? Weren't you afraid to go back to your house because you left because of fear?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I left because I was afraid, but I was just as afraid in Rovna as I was at home. So I thought, "Well, it doesn't really matter whether I'm at Rovna or at home. I'm still afraid, wherever I am."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you came back home in the morning?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the third day, that is, the 19th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to say "the 18th."

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 18th in the morning, you came home. Did you see these people around your house on that day whom you had seen before?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I arrived on that day, I saw them in the depression, not right away in the morning, but after I had seen to my livestock. I looked for something to eat because I had had nothing to eat the previous day and night, and then I saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they? Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were moving up to my house to make a telephone call and back to the depression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you see?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I saw my son Mirko Sakic. I saw Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic, Miro Vidovic, the late Miro Vidovic, Dragan Vidovic, Dragan Samija, and I don't remember seeing anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that third day, did they go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the third day, maybe in the afternoon, they moved up the road toward the Kupreskic houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who led them?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know who led them there. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone take you up there above the village of Pirici and Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, after the conflict broke out, seven, eight, ten days later, all the elderly people, including me, were taken to that line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at that line?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I stayed in the trench for a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the only person who was rather elderly who was taken there, or were there others from the village who were the same age as you who were taken up there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there were people older than me and people my age, as well as younger people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the line, you were in the trench?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we were in the trench.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few more questions about your neighbours. Do you know Sakib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know Sakib Ahmic well, his whole family, from his father and his generation. I know less about the younger generation, about the children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are your relations with Sakib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never had any kind of quarrel or conflict with that man in my whole life. His father, when I was building my first house, helped me, and I am still grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Sakib Ahmic like as a person? You say you never had a conflict with him.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I didn't, but his Muslim neighbours had problems with him, and as I say, I never did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of problems did his neighbours have with him?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he used to fight. Then he divorced his wife. He built fences on other people's land, and in the end, he moved to the basement of his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do in the basement?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he had one or two rooms. I don't know. I never went in, but I know he lived in the basement because he told me that himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he liked to drink alcohol? Did he have any problems because of that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we would often get drunk together at my house, and I know that he was even treated for alcoholism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, just before the conflict in March or April, did you see him?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. When did you find out how many of your Muslim neighbours were killed on the 16th? Did you find out then or later?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I found out, and most of the Croatian population found out that unfortunately a lot of people were killed when they started taking away the bodies to be buried, but during the first three or four days, I didn't know how many people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who did that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know who didn't do it, but I don't know who did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who didn't?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I can say now that these people who are here didn't do it, but I don't know who did. But that's what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to ask that D104/2 be taken into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Krajina:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sakic.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will put a few questions to you connected to the accused Vlatko Kupreskic. To begin with, could you tell us whether you knew Vlatko and his family?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know Vlatko's father, mother, even his grandfather. I have known Vlatko ever since he was born.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you know what Vlatko Kupreskic did for a living in 1992, 1993, and what activities he engaged in before and during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Vlatko had always tried to be a businessman, and he was then engaged in business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you know if Vlatko was mobilised then or at any time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Vlatko was not mobilised, and he couldn't have been mobilised, because of his health. I know that he had heart surgery, and that he did not serve in the former JNA, and that he did not participate in the war that occurred in our part of the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us whether you have ever seen Vlatko Kupreskic in uniform or carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Throughout the war, I never saw Vlatko in any kind of uniform except in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know whether Vlatko Kupreskic was active in politics? Did he ever play a prominent part in any political rallies?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think he didn't have time because of his business, and I think he didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever belong to any kind of political organisation?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, whether Vlatko had any kind of negative attitude toward Muslims, his neighbours and other Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't tell you names, but I know that he had a lot of Muslims who were friends who came to his home. His house was closer to the Muslim houses than mine was, and I know he had a lot of Muslim friends and that he never had any problems with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now talk about the 16th of April, the day when the conflict broke out. You said that on that day, you were in your home the whole day until 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You probably know, but let me ask you, where is the house of Vlatko Kupreskic exactly?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there is a path leading from Vlatko Kupreskic's house to your house and further on in the direction of Jozo Vrebac's house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there is. I know it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that path pass by your house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You can come up to my house by car, but from my house, you have to take a footpath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but when you are going from Vlatko Kupreskic's house to Jozo's house, do you have to pass by your house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, you have to pass by my house and then go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, on the 16th of April, 1993, did you see, on the path or road that we have just talked about, that Vlatko or some members of his family passed by the house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Vlatko, his wife, two children, and mother passed by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was about 5.00, half past five. I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You saw them well?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was on the edge of the asphalt road, and they passed about one and a half metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how he was dressed at that time, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in civilian clothes, as he was always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, the 16th of April, 1993, did you see Vlatko again, Vlatko Kupreskic? And if you did, when was it?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw him at about half past ten, when he was going back from the direction of Jozo Vrebac's shelter and I was standing beside my garage. So I said, "Where are you going, Vlatko," because you could hear gunfire from behind his house. And he said, "My father stayed behind. I have to see him." His father was ill. He had broken his leg, and on that morning they were unable to evacuate him from the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long Vlatko stayed with you, or did he stay, or did he continue towards his house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I tried to persuade him not to go because I thought it was too dangerous for him to go there. So I tried to get him to come into my house, into the ground floor, and we stayed there for about an hour, an hour and a half, but then he insisted on going to his house to see his father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time was it, about?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, about half past 12.00, 1.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So he left?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He went in the direction of his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, throughout this time when Vlatko came, until about half past 12.00 or 1.00 when he left your house, do you know that he was there all the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we talked. Well, we didn't talk all the time, we were also silent, but we looked at one another. We were together all time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the last time that you saw Vlatko on that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, on that day. I didn't see him again that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, let us summarise. Can we say, on the basis of what you have said, that on the 16th of April, 1993, you saw on two occasions, in the morning between half past 5.00 and 6.00 and from about half past 11.00 to about half past 12.00 or 1.00, you personally were with Vlatko, and Vlatko at that time was in your house without interruption. Can we conclude this?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I can guarantee this with my life, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Sakic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Terrier: Good morning, Mr. Sakic. My name is Franck Terrier, and I'm one of the representatives of the Prosecution in this case. I think that you were told that I would also put questions to you which you will need to answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, I would like us to talk about the responsibility that you had within the civilian defence which you talked about yesterday. You said that in your neighbourhood, your part of the village, you were responsible for civilian defence, and on the 16th of April, just like on the 20th of October, you were in charge of informing your neighbours about what was going to happen. Do you remember stating that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. But this wasn't civil defence. We, at our own initiative, divided ourselves within the village in order to be able to inform the people more easily, those who were living closer to our houses, because during the bombardment of Vitez and Busovaca we organised ourselves, so then we would at each alert call people to come to the shelter. So when we got this information, we would inform people to come to the shelter. There was no other kind of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that this was an agreement, an organisation, amongst yourselves and others. Who were these other people that you had agreements with, that you organised yourselves with?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't make an agreement with anybody or organise with anybody. On two occasions I was informed, for the first time by the late Jozo Tomic Bobas and the second time by Dragan Vidovic, that I had to tell the population to go to the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understood that well, Mr. Sakic, but I wanted to know who, for example, entrusted you with the task of informing the population of those ten houses in your part of the village. You said that yesterday. You said that you were in charge of informing people who lived in some ten houses in your neighbourhood. So now I would like to know who told you that, and how were you organised in this sense?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, like I said, we organised in that way -- well, like I said, I was informed by those people. I don't know who they received some other kind of information from. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, that was not my question. I understood well who you informed that you needed to go to the shelter. What I would like to know is who entrusted you with informing the families who lived in those ten houses?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, let me say it again. The first time I was woken up by Jozo Bobas, the second time by Dragan Vidovic, and I then alerted the citizens to come to the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will pose the question in a different way. You told us yesterday that you were entrusted with duties regarding civilian defence. Maybe that wasn't strictly civilian defence in the strict meaning of that term, but amongst your duties you also were entrusted -- for example, in case of a fire or war, danger -- you were entrusted with informing the families who lived in your part of the village. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question is the following. Mr. Sakic, who entrusted you with this? Who entrusted you with the duty of informing these families?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, who entrusted me with informing the families? Well, Ivica Vidovic was there, his nickname was Jevco, and I got that from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's not mention Ivica Vidovic for the time being. Let's forget him. I will try to put the question again to you. For example, if there had been a fire -- and this is possible, isn't it? -- were you the person who was charged in that case with informing the families? I think you said something like that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I will ask you several questions about the meetings that were held in the school in Ahmici following the first conflict. You attended the first meeting, that's what you told us, in the course of which about 150 people were present, and about 55 or 60 of those people were Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that that meeting was spontaneous. Could you tell us some of the people who spoke at that meeting, at that first meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Hazim Ahmic Hadzija spoke, Ivo Josipovic, Hajrudin Pjanic, Abdulah Ahmic, and many others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That first meeting, was any of the accused present at that meeting, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about the second meeting now. You told us that the second meeting was attended by Pero Skopljak and Ivica Santic, among others, as far as I understood, and like you said, those two people chaired the meeting, they conducted the meeting?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They didn't conduct the meeting. Mr. Kajmovic was there as well. But they didn't conduct the meeting. They simply observed how we would reach agreement, how we would talk, and to try to direct us, but there was no official meeting. Nobody officially conducted the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second meeting, was it attended by any of the accused?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean they were not there, or that you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the second meeting, did the Croat population of Ahmici speak, did members of the Croat population --

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, everybody who wanted to speak, anybody who knew anything positive or nice, they talked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what the Croat population, members of the Croat population, those who spoke at the second meeting, do you remember what they said?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I know what I asked, but I don't know what the others said. A long time has passed, so I don't remember what they said. But mainly positive things were said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. But, Mr. Sakic, yesterday you very specifically talked about some things about -- for example, Sulejman Ahmic and what people said at that meeting, that there were also some extremist speeches, and you quoted some of them, and I think, according to your memory, you could probably tell us what the Croats who attended that meeting said.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What the Croats were saying, I don't know exactly what the Croats who were there were saying, but I know what the Muslims who were at the meeting said, and I can say exactly what the Muslims said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that yesterday already, Mr. Sakic, so we don't need to repeat that. I just wanted to note that you remember what the Muslims said very well, but you don't remember anything that the Croats said.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember the nice things that the Muslims said, but the not-so-nice things that the Muslims said have stayed with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about the guards now that you participated in, in the period between October of '92 and April of '93. You told us that you took part in those village guards, and that you had a hunting rifle. Could you tell us how were the guards organised and who organised them?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The village guards were not organised by anyone. They were on our own initiative. That means you could go and not go. There was nobody that we were responsible to or there was no order in this regard. They were just something spontaneous that happened in the population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, I understood that the guards functioned on a democratic principle and that this was voluntary. I wanted to know who decided that evening, for example, that you would be on guard duty, and then on some other evening some other person? Who made these decisions?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Simply, we would just agree. One evening, the late Anto Kupreskic came, the father of Zoran and Mirjan, and he would say, "Well, why don't the two of us go on guard tonight?" So I would take my hunting rifle. We would walk around until we were tired, and then we would come back home. We were not relieved by anyone, neither did we relieve anybody. That's how these night watches were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your son Mirko take part in the village guards?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I think he did, in the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think or you're certain? Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I didn't hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your son have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of weapon?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Some kind of a gun, a Kalashnikov or something. I don't know what it's called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know where he got the weapon from?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he is not underage. I don't know where he got the weapon from. Well, he was here so he probably told you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order for the transcript to be clear, I will ask you the question that I asked you awhile ago. I asked you, "Did you see your son taking part in the village guard?" I'm asking you this question again because it's not in the record.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not see him, but I know that he did go to the village guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we will move to the 16th of April. You told us that you were woken up by Dragan Vidovic, that you went out of your house, and you went to wake up the different people that you mentioned. Among those people, you mentioned, I think, Miralem Strmonja; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did Miralem Strmonja and his family live? Could you please tell us? Maybe it's a little difficult for you to find your way on this photograph. Maybe you don't have to indicate it on the aerial map, but maybe you can explain to us where and how far from your house did Miralem Strmonja live?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, gladly. This map is very inconvenient for me. Miralem Strmonja was maybe 250 metres away from my house, going towards Zume from my house. If necessary, I will try to indicate it on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The south is up; the north is down. If you think that you can find it, it may be good for you to point it out for us.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's here -- no, it's here. Here it is (indicating). Two of his brothers-in-law are there, and he's there in their house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that, very quickly, at about 4.30 a.m., people gathered in front of your house. Would you please sit down, Mr. Sakic? You said, Mr. Sakic, that at around 4.30, people gathered in front of your house. Was it planned, in case of an alert or problem, for people who were there to collect in front of your house? Was that organised? Was this planned in advance?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was not planned in advance, but before the bombardment, my basement was set aside, even though it was small, as a safe shelter. So we knew several times before to come without any kind of alert. People would just say somebody told them. Five or six of them would come in front of the basement, and then if nothing happened, they would go back to their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then we can say that there was some kind of organisation in case of an alert or a danger and that people, and specially those who were living in your neighbourhood, knew exactly where they had to go in case of danger or in case of an alert?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, if a person was in danger, of course, he had to find a shelter for himself. They would find my house a safe place, and this is where they would come to take shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about the soldiers who passed in front of your house between 4.00 and 4.30 in the morning. You said that those soldiers were wearing insignia, but you didn't say what kind of insignia. Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know how to behave in this situation. The Prosecutor is talking about other times than the times mentioned by the witness. He didn't say they gathered in front of his house at 4.30. So is the Prosecutor doing this on purpose, trying to confuse the witness? I don't know. I'm not sure whether I should intervene or not, but the wrong times are being mentioned all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If I have made a mistake ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: If I have made a mistake, I am willing to correct it. I believe it was in good faith because Mr. Sakic talked about people meeting in front of his house at half past four. I may have made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Ms. Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, I am not trying to create problems, but he never mentioned anything in front of his house at 4.30, and he never talked about soldiers at this time. The times are essentially different. I don't know what you see on your transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Terrier's last question as regards soldiers was not connected to the time, to 4.30. He didn't say that the witness saw the soldiers at 4.30. I seem to remember that the witness mentioned the soldiers and that he saw them between 4.30 and 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That's what I said. We will ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, at what time, as far as you can remember, you saw soldiers in front of your house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At about twenty minutes to -- 5.30; that's when they passed by my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, I will put my question again. Yesterday, and I'm certain of this, you mentioned that the soldiers were wearing insignia on their uniforms. Can you tell us today what the insignia were?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I will tell you. They had white belts and pistol casings, holsters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have any insignia showing what unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't notice that, but I noticed some kind of bands tied to their shoulders. They were painted, their faces were painted, so I couldn't recognise any of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned bands on their shoulders, were they coloured bands?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were coloured. I couldn't see very well, but I could see that there were bands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how long they were, these bands?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, 20, 30 centimetres, perhaps, like this (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the colour of these bands?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I can't specify because of the prevailing conditions and because I was in a state of shock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these soldiers say anything to you, ask you anything?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, they didn't ask anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you think, considering the route they were taking, that they knew the location very well?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, most probably they did; however, at that moment, I didn't think about anything. I was just wondering where they were going with those weapons and the paint on their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If not at that moment, but did you think later perhaps that the soldiers you met on the road either knew the place well and were well informed of the situation on the ground or that one or more persons who knew the place well were guiding them? Did you think that, maybe not at that moment but a little later?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I'm thinking about it now, and if they hadn't known the road to take, they would have asked for instructions, but I would have recognised someone who was guiding them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us make this quite clear: On the spot where you saw them, the road ends; therefore, someone who didn't know the terrain would find it hard to find what way to continue?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us recall the depression, which is located behind your house and which is entered along the path that goes by your garage. Can you tell us the exact time it takes on foot to reach the Kupreskic group of houses from your house? Can you tell us how long it would take?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It depends on how fast you walk, but you can get there in five or six minutes, maybe even sooner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, it's a very short distance.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that morning, was it raining?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know there was snow, but I don't know whether it was raining. I know there was snow, but I don't know if there was any precipitation. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are talking about the 16th of April, 1993, Mr. Sakic, and you say that it was snowing?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. There was snow on the ground. I didn't say snow was falling. I didn't say it was snowing. I just said that there was snow on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was snow on the ground. How much snow? How deep was it?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, something like this (indicating). There was a little snow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show me the depth of the snow because I couldn't see very well?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Like that (indicating), that much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ten centimetres?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, ten in places, five in places, none in other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. Are you certain?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I'm certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, can you explain why some people, including your son Mirko and Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, considered it useful or necessary to take refuge in the depression behind your house, and how could this depression, with snow on the ground, be a shelter in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This depression is about 30 to 40 metres away from my house and my garage. The configuration of the terrain is such that small arms fire cannot hit anything in it, so they felt it was safe. However, they could see our house from it, they could see other houses behind, and they were close to the Kupreskic houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in this depression you could feel safe only if you were certain that no enemy would come to the edge of the depression or enter the depression and that the fighting was taking place at a certain distance?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there was no really safe place, but this was one of the safest places for people who were outdoors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other condition for someone to feel safe in that depression is that they would be sure that no shell from a mortar launcher or a cannon could land there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, of course a shell could land there, but you weren't safe in a basement from that. You weren't safe anywhere from shells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't you think that in a basement with a concrete ceiling you would feel a little safer from a shell?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you would feel a little safer, but if I had felt safe in my basement, I wouldn't have left it. I'd have stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say, Mr. Sakic, that the people in the depression were safer in the depression, in the open, than they would have been in a basement?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know how they felt or how safe they felt, but as regards safety, it seems to me that the people in the basement were no safer than the people in the depression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony yesterday, you mentioned your son Slavko. Your son Slavko was living with you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He has his own house next to my house and Mirko's house. My son Mirko and I have a house which is divided into two, and he has a house next to ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did your son Slavko do for a living at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean during the war or in peacetime? I didn't understand you well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April '93, what was your son Slavko doing? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My son Slavko was in PZO. He was in the anti-aircraft defence, and he joined it when the Serbian aggression started against Slovenia and then against Croatia and then against Bosnia. He was in the anti-aircraft defence, PZO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is the place you call "PZO"? Is that a place or a military unit? Could you explain this to us?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it's a unit. The letters "PZO" mean "anti-aircraft defence."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. On the 16th of April, in the morning, where was your son Slavko?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Slavko wasn't at home. He was in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Where in Vitez? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know he was in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, whenever he left, I asked him where he was going, and he always said, "I'm going to the PZO." That's what he would answer when I asked him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he leave?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether he left a day before, two days before, that morning. I can't remember exactly the time when he left. It wasn't that morning, but it was before that morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you be sure that he wasn't there that morning?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Where, in the house?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I woke up my daughter-in-law and his two children, so I know that he wasn't at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you thought that he was in Vitez because he wasn't at home?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your son was a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't say he was a member of the HVO. I said he was a member of that PZO before the war, and he remained there until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that anti-aircraft defence unit, under whose command was it?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a uniform did he have?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he had a regular military camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a while ago that, in front of your house, at about 5.00, 5.30 a.m. -- I think I'm not making a mistake regarding the time now -- you saw Vlatko Kupreskic and his family, and they were going towards the shelter. You said that at 10.30 or around 10.30, you again saw Vlatko Kupreskic, who was coming back from the shelter in the Vrebac house. As far as you can remember, is it quite clear that Vlatko Kupreskic, between your house and the Vrebac shelter, that he was taking the most direct route?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was no closer route than by my house, from his house to the house of Jozo Vrebac and back. There was no other shorter road that he could take on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you can remember and as far as you know, he was walking along the road that everybody had taken, obviously, which leads from your house to Zume?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was no other road. He was going from my house in the direction of Zume. He was going from his house, passed by my house and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that Vlatko Kupreskic was concerned about his father, but he spent about an hour or an hour and a half with you and that at about 12.30 or 1.00, he left, so this is approximately the time. But you claim that when he came from the Vrebac shelter, that Vlatko Kupreskic stopped at your place, stayed there for awhile, before he continued on his way to his house towards the Kupreskic houses?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in your house during all of that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Occasionally, I was outside. I was in the house, and occasionally, I was outside because it was not possible then to sit in one place because you were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were you in the basement? Were you in your basement, you and Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. We were in the house, in the kitchen, the two of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So practically all the time, you were in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, we lost a little time while we were talking in front of the garage and while we were entering the house, and then we sat in the house for a little bit, and then we came back. So we spent that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you are aware of the fact that, since you were not in the basement or in the depression, you were not in any kind of shelter?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I had the shelter. The garage is like this (indicating) and the shed in relation to where the action was, and because of that, nothing can happen to the house. You can see that in the photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were other people there with you?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, no, only Vlatko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for an hour to an hour and a half, you remained in the kitchen or in front of the garage, you and Vlatko Kupreskic, and nobody else saw you together?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you talk about, can you remember, you and Vlatko Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you we were more quiet, and we just looked at one another out of fear. We didn't talk about anything in particular that was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, do you remember, in January '98, you gave a statement, which the Prosecution received from the Defence. You say in that statement that at around 10.00 a.m., Vlatko appeared in front of your house because, according to what you understood, he had to help in the evacuation of the wounded. He remained there for about three hours, and because there were no wounded, he left. Do you remember making that statement?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When Vlatko came back -- excuse me. When he came back from the Vrebac shelter, I was thinking the following: Since he was unfit for military duty, he was not a member of any army or any political or social organisation, I thought that -- this is my personal opinion -- and because he has a driver's license, if necessary, he could provide medical assistance. That's my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your personal opinion, the opinion that you expressed; on the 16th of April, 1993, since he was not physically fit for active military duty and he had a driver's license, he was supposed to help in the evacuation of the wounded. But if somebody is fit for military duty, then he would be assigned to some kind of military unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your son Mirko physically fit for duty?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under those conditions, which military unit did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You're thinking of my son Mirko?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm thinking of your son Mirko.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he didn't belong to any unit, just like I did not belong to any military unit. In the same way, he did not belong to any military unit at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, should we take our break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, a 30-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, let me go back for a few moments to the statement that you made in January of 1998. As I said a little while ago, you said that Vlatko, according to what you heard, was at your house because he was supposed to help to evacuate the wounded, and I was asking you to tell us who told you that. Apparently nobody said -- that was an idea that you had. Vlatko didn't say anything; is that correct? He didn't say anything? Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic did not say that he was responsible for evacuating the wounded? Or did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I thought, myself, that he was entrusted with driving somebody, but this didn't happen, and then when he came to my house, I saw that he was talking about his father and that he was shaken up by everything that was happening, and I then saw that there was no duty that he was charged with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Sakic, that was in January of 1998 that you said that that's what you were thinking. Was there anything else that might have made you think that? Did he have any material with him? Did he have an automobile not far away? Was there something else that might have made you think that that was his mission, that is, to evacuate the wounded?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I thought, because he was unfit for military duty, like I said before, because was not a member of any unit, I didn't exclusively think that he only had to drive Croats or Muslims, but nothing came out of that. This was my personal opinion. I didn't hear anything from anyone regarding this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you thought that morning was that all the Croats who were of an age where they could do something useful had a mission to carry out?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wasn't thinking about that. I only was thinking about Vlatko at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that Vlatko Kupreskic was dressed in civilian clothing. Do you remember more specifically how he was dressed -- that is, what colour his clothing was? If you don't remember, just please tell us that you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I remember, when I think back about him, civilian needle cord, thick cord pants, and he had a civilian jacket. But I don't remember what kind of a jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The English transcript does not quite correspond with the French version. Could you please repeat how Vlatko Kupreskic was dressed on that morning, as best as you can recall.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said he had a jacket. I don't know what colour it was. It was a civilian jacket. The trousers were corduroy, long cord stripes. That's what we call them, at least. Thick cord.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us a little while ago that Mr. Kupreskic had stayed in your house between 1.00 and 1.30. When you testified in writing, you spoke about 3.00. As specifically as you can, or as precisely as you can, could you clarify that.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Maybe the person who was taking the statement took it down wrong, because -- or maybe I expressed myself wrongly, but it is the way I say it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Vlatko Kupreskic left, in what direction was he going, as best as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was going in the direction of his house because he said he was going to his house. He went behind my garage toward his house, and I returned to the house. Then I couldn't see him any more. I couldn't see Vlatko any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he went behind your garage, and then he went down into the depression?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point, as far as you know, did your son Mirko, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, among others, at that point, were they in the depression?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The depression is divided between two paths. One goes straight towards Vlatko's house, and the depression is semi to the left. So I don't know whether you could see it or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what time and how many times you yourself went to the depression on that morning, or rather, during that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly the time, but I went at least three or four times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the depression on three or four occasions on that day, where were the people that you met in the depression? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were in the depression. It's not large. They were sitting around on whatever they had to sit on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they far from your house, or that part of the depression which is near your house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where they were in respect of your house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's a depression which is above my house. I said it was 30 or 40 metres away, and then somewhere in the middle, I would use to find them closer to the house. Sometimes they would be farther from the house. They weren't only sitting down. Perhaps they were nervous. They were walking around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a document that was given to us by the Defence, which is a summary of your testimony, it is indicated that different people who were in the depression -- and specifically your son, Mirko Sakic, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic -- that they came to your house on several occasions during that day. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that they made some telephone calls.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whom they were calling?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Since my son worked for UNPROFOR, and he knew a woman who knew the language of that unit, and he was trying to call her so that they could take Bilic Ramo and Zijad Strmonja out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean in order to evacuate the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not evacuate them, but these three families, to take them out somewhere, to a safer place. We were afraid, so to a safer place than the one where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why the Muslims and not the Croats?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, because there were few of them there, and because we heard gunfire in Ahmici, and we were afraid that they might get hurt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Mr. Sakic, doesn't that mean that in your mind, that there were Muslims that were near you, and not the Croats?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, according to what happened, they were in greater danger than the Croats were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew that on that day, on the 16th of April, in the morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't know what was going to happen at all, or who was going to get hurt. Because had I known, I had very good friends, I would have told them even at the risk of my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your house, Mr. Sakic, could you see toward the direction of the main road going from Busovaca to Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Busovaca-Vitez road cannot be seen from my house directly because there's a lot of shrubbery. But I know where it is, and you can hear vehicles passing along that road from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your house, could you see the houses that were between you and the road, or some of the houses?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, for instance, see the house of the Karic family?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see Nadira or Besim Ahmic's house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, the two Muslim houses closest to my house were those of Refik Ahmic and Sulejman Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that morning, during that day, around those Muslim houses that were between yours and the main road, did you see soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those houses are about 150 metres away from my house, and when they came in, I saw that, and that house burnt down. Refik Ahmic was -- they left 20 years ago and lived in another house, and they used this house only as a holiday home, and I didn't see them entering the second house, but it burnt down like the first one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw soldiers going into a house which then burned?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you -- take all the time you need if it's difficult -- could I ask you to show us approximately on the photograph where that house was that you saw burning and into which you saw soldiers going. Could you find it on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if possible, perhaps this map might be turned upside down for the witness, because then it would be much easier for him to find the house. He gets confused, so maybe it will be simpler if we turn the map upside down so that Ahmici is--

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, it's all right. I know this. I'm not confused any more. You don't have to turn it upside down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Well, if the witness wants it to be left the way it is, that's all right.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is my house (indicating), this is Refik Ahmic's house (indicating), and this is Sulejman Ahmic's house (indicating). This is Refik Ahmic's, this is Sulejman Ahmic's, and this whole plot of land was their family inheritance, and they sold part of it, and this is the area I saw and where I saw what happened to these houses. This is Refik's house, this is Sulejman's house, and this is mine. It's about 150 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear, Mr. Sakic. Could you tell us exactly what time it was that you saw the soldiers going into the house?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was on the 16th, but I can't tell you the exact time it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the morning, the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly. I don't know, really. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that area that you showed us, did you see any people who lived there, any inhabitants, running away or moving about? People who lived there.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw the Muslim inhabitants of Donja Zume going this way, in the direction of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show us that, please?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
