utterances.text: Here (indicating) in Donja Zume, and they were taking this route. There is a road here, not an important one, and they took that road and went in the direction of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know because two or three would pass by at a time. They were not organised in a file so that they could be counted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Sakic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, just a moment please because the witness didn't have his headset on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, did you know that in that area that you showed us, that six Muslims were killed? Ibrahim Karic --

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my close --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ibrahim Karic, Nadira and Besim Ahmic, Sahabudin Osmancevic, and Esad and Hajrija Ahmic. Did you know that all of those people had been killed that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't know that and I didn't find out their names. This is the first time actually that I have heard the names of the people who were killed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that on the second day at around 8.00 or 9.00 in the evening, correct me if I'm wrong, you said that you left the shelter, where you had found refuge, in order to go back. On the road that you took going back, did you look around you, and if you did, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me tell you. When we set out between 20.00 and 21.00 in the evening from Luka Vidovic's warehouse, on the main road, the group that had been in Jozo Vrebac's house caught up with us. Then a column, more or less a file was formed, and we went on together. When we arrived at Radak's Bridge, I saw some armed people on the other side of the bridge. It was dark. I was carrying my two-year-old grandson in my arms. I didn't recognise anyone. I didn't pay much attention until we arrived at the house where they spent the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few minutes ago, Mr. Sakic, you spoke very unfavourably about Sakib Ahmic, and you said that "he would come to my house and we would both drink and both of us were drunk"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes -- no, I'm not saying that we were drunk, but we would have a drink together. He would drink with me, and he was always on very good terms with me personally. But I heard from other people, including his close relatives, that he was a difficult man. As regards our personal relations, we were on very good terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, could you please tell us whether you were on bad terms with any Muslim in the village?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, there were no Muslims in the village with whom I ever had any kind of conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any quarrels with the Croats in the village?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Do I have to say that? There is a man, a Croat in the village, with whom I am not speaking, even today, but it doesn't matter who he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there is one man with whom you have had problems?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself to be a tolerant person, a person who is not prone to arguing?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I think I'm more tolerant than not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that your Muslim neighbours have started returning to the village, now that they are back, do you encounter them sometimes?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean when Ahmici is being rebuilt?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I encounter these people. Individuals came to my house, those who were my family friends, like Sulejman Ahmic who had a house below mine. We meet, we say hello, and we have a chat, just as we did before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do any of your Muslim neighbours hold what happened in Ahmici against you? Do they tell you that they think you are responsible?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not me personally. They all tell me that they are trying not to talk about it and that they hope it will never happen again, but none of the ones that I have talked to ever made any direct accusations against anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The two neighbours you mentioned as having houses close to yours?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Refik and Sulejman?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Which of them was in the village on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Neither of them because, as I said, Refik lives in Visoko and uses this house only on weekends, and Sulejman has a flat in Vitez, and he built this for retirement in his old age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You also said that, had you known anything about the attack, you would have told some people, even at the risk of your life. Which people were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I would have told Esad Ahmic, Hajrudin Pjanic. I would have rang up Sulejman in Vitez. There are other people whom I would have told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean you would have telephoned your Muslim friends, had you known?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Well, I didn't have a telephone, so I would have gone to tell them personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the reason you didn't call them because you didn't have a telephone or because you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I've just told you. I would have gone personally to tell them, since I didn't have a telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know where Mirjan Santic is from?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mirjan Santic is from the village of Santici which joins Zume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's the neighbouring village to Pirici?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is Mirjan Santic's house from the houses of the Kupreskics; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, about a kilometre and a half along the road, 1.500 metres if you take the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at this map and say whether you can see where Mirjan Santic's house is, if you can? If you can't, we won't ask you to do it, but could you tell us whether you can see it?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No, I can't. I'm certain of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned Ivica Vidovic, also known as Jevco, when the Prosecutor asked you about the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Ivica Vidovic, Jevco, in the civil defence?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what his post was in the civil defence, but he said to me, "You take care of these 10 to 15 houses; Ivo Vidovic will take care of another 10 to 15 houses," and so on. I didn't have any other duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the anti-aircraft defence of which your son was a member, your son Slavko Sakic, as you told us, do you remember when it was organised?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was organised, if you remember, I said that, when the Serbian aggression against Slovenia and Croatia began. That's when it was organised and came into being. I don't know the year now. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means it was organised before the Serbian aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether this anti-aircraft defence had any connections with the SPS factory in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I never worked in Vitez. I worked in the Zenica ironworks, so I don't know what they did in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you did at the ironworks in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I worked at the furnaces. I was a smelter, and I worked there for 40 years. I retired in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see your son, Mirko Sakic, keeping guard?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him, but I know he went. He went once or twice, I'm not sure exactly, but he did go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he didn't go all the time?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. No one went all the time. No one had to go all the time. You could simply find a friend or a neighbour and patrol the village a few times and then go home and go to bed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when your son started working for the humanitarian organisation?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know the exact time. All I know is that it was before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, was Mirko away from home often?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. He's a grown man. I can't have any influence on him. I don't know where he goes and what he does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But you could see whether he was going on a business trip, if he was away for a few days; could you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember if I saw that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please also tell us, the depression that we talked about, can you see when a person walks along the path which leads from the Kupreskic houses? Can you see from the depression if somebody is taking that road?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The one that leads from the warehouse towards my house, is that the one you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. From the Kupreskic houses.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, from the Kupreskic houses, well, you can see partially if something is coming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Sakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: I will be very brief in order to clarify some matters. Re-examined by Mr. Krajina:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sakic, the question by the Prosecution, you said that, on the 16th of April, 1993, there was snow. Yes. You were indicating that there was maybe five centimetres of snow. Could you be more specific? Could you tell us whether there was any snow on the road?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was no snow on the road, but there was snow in the depressions. Where there was more shadow, there was a little bit of snow there, but the snow did not cover the whole ground or the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just one more sub-question: This is quite a high section; this is not a plain, the region where Pirici is. So you could have a kind of sprinkling of snow, patches of snow?

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I meant. Those patches of snow, we called them that too, they would remain perhaps until the beginning of May in such configurations of terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no questions for the witness. Mr. Sakic, thank you so much for coming to The Hague to give evidence. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the next witness, let me quickly deal with two housekeeping matters. First of all, we received a motion filed on the 16th of March and submitted by Counsel Radovic and Slokovic-Glumac about Mrs. Samija, the substitution of Mrs. Dragica Samija for Mrs. Kata Samija. The motion is granted. The second matter, we hope that you don't mind if we hold the afternoon sitting on Monday, next Monday, instead of Wednesday? Is that fine? We will bring forward the afternoon sitting. We will be sitting on Monday morning and afternoon, Tuesday morning, Wednesday morning, and Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just briefly say, we will reduce our list of witnesses, and probably tomorrow we will be provide a list for you for the second week where there will be fewer witnesses. I believe that we will finish with all of our witnesses in the second week. I would like to know, if we call the remaining five or six witnesses, whether on Thursday the Defence of Vlatko Kupreskic should begin on Thursday or should we leave that for the beginning of April? Because I think that we will probably give up more than half of our witnesses. There was a plan for us to have the whole of that week and then also a week at the end of April. Now we have changed our plan, and we will definitely agree today with the Victims and Witnesses Unit that we will not have so many witnesses and that we will probably finish with the Defence in the second week. Then there is the technical question, whether the Defence of Vlatko Kupreskic should begin in the second week or should we leave that for the beginning of April? They will start with witnesses who are more important and who will need more time, so they would not want to have that interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: When you say "second week," you mean next week? Because you anticipate that you would probably finish with your witnesses by Wednesday, Wednesday at 1.30?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: If we work on that afternoon, then under our programme, that would be on Wednesday. Well, we never know how the Prosecution will react and how long their cross-examination will be. We have a kind of review of witnesses, and we believe that we will have that number and that we will be finished by Wednesday. But we are interested, as far as the Vlatko Kupreskic Defence is concerned, they intend to start with witnesses that will take more time, so should we leave that for next week or should we leave that for the beginning of April?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: If I may say something on this matter too, we're meeting with the Victims and Witnesses Unit, and, as my colleague Ms. Slokovic-Glumac said, the first witness we intend to call is the President of the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina who will testify about Count 1. Our position is such that we have discussed that with the unit, that it may happen that he will start his testimony on Thursday and will not finish, or he may not even have time to start on Thursday because we don't know when the witnesses for Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic's Defence will finish. We have made different kinds of arrangements with the unit to have this witness wait or to have him brought urgently to The Hague, which is all pretty complicated. In a way, it doesn't really suit us or the witness. A representative of the unit perhaps said that he would discuss this problem with the Trial Chamber, I don't know if he had already contacted you, but we are having this meeting today. It is in the interests of the Defence of Vlatko Kupreskic to bring out their evidence in its entirety. We would like to start that in April so that we're not brought into the position with a witness that we consider important, that we begin, and interrupt, and then begin again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think we agree with the point made by Counsel Par. I think it's better for the Defence counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic to have a few days in a row, a period of time. It would not be good for you to start with one witness and then maybe to go on, even to stop before he has finished. Therefore, let us try to finish on Wednesday or Thursday with the witnesses called by Counsel Radovic and Slokovic-Glumac. Probably we will need three or four days. On the other hand, I've got some bad news for you and for us as well; namely, we will not be able to sit in Kupreskic in April because we three Judges, we are busy in other cases. Judge Mumba and I are in a particular case, and Judge May in another case. We will, therefore, have to put off our hearings until the 3rd of May. We will start on the 3rd of May, so we are going to lose four days, four working days. Remember, we had decided to sit in Kupreskic for four days towards the end of April. We will try to catch up, maybe either in May or in June, so that we can find time to try to finish by, say, July or by September. Probably, there is some hope that we may finish by July, by the end of July, so that we can take some time to draft the judgment. Therefore, we will start with the witnesses for Vlatko Kupreskic on the 3rd of May. You can make arrangements with the unit so that they can come here on the 3rd of May. By the way, Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, did I understand you correctly when you said that you have shortened your list, but next week, we will have a few more witnesses, in addition to probably one on the present list? I hope that we can finish with these two remaining witnesses this week, today and tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Next week, we plan to finish with the eight remaining witnesses. We will give up the rest, but the witnesses who will be here next week will be much shorter because they will only testify to certain circumstances. These will be brief testimonies, and we will be able to finish that by Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I only have one question. I see that court witnesses have already been called for the 26th of April of this year. I wanted to know what will happen with that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Court witnesses, I think, for Vlatko -- these are the three -- no, for Mr. Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: For Josipovic, there are three witnesses altogether, I think, three court witnesses which have been called for the 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We have to reschedule this because, of course, it would be awkward to have them on the 3rd of May and then the witnesses for Vlatko Kupreskic. We will probably put off -- when are you going to call your witnesses, the other ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: After the witnesses for Vlatko Kupreskic, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will first hear the witnesses for Vlatko Kupreskic, and then we will call the court witnesses, plus the other witnesses you yourself are going to call.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, two of those witnesses are ours, two court witnesses were also called at our request, but the time for their testimony was the 26th of April. It's the same day. One of the witnesses is a joint witness. Perhaps we could finish with those witnesses because they are common witnesses for Kupreskics, for Santic, and Josipovic. These are joint witnesses. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Possibly a good solution could consist of first of all calling two out of three court witnesses, those two court witnesses who are common to the brothers Kupreskic, Mirjan and Zoran, and also the other two, Mr. Josipovic and so on. We will first hear those two. Then we will move on to witnesses for Vlatko Kupreskic. Then at the end, before we start with your witnesses, we call the third witness who, if I understood you correctly, only relates to Mr. Josipovic. Is it fine with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, the third witness is for the Defence counsel Petar Pavkovic. Two witnesses are for Josipovic and for the Kupreskic brothers. I will say this again. Two witnesses have been called for the 26th of April. I think those are the witnesses Ajanovic and another person, SA. These two witnesses need to be questioned first, and then the third witness should be questioned after that. I think that would be a good way. The third witness is the wife. I'm just saying the names that we got in the information, that I was informed by the Court that this would be court witnesses. I have been informed about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that we should then call the three court witnesses? No? Or -- I didn't understand you. First, on the 3rd of May, the three court witnesses, then move on to the witnesses to be called by Vlatko Kupreskic, and then go back to the other ones, to your --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I only referred to the two witnesses who have been called for the 26th of April of this year, but in your decision I think you had placed the third witness -- you confused him, and you placed him first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. Thank you. I would like to take up a point just made by Judge Mumba, a very good point, that we should not now decide on this matter, in order not to waste time, and maybe you can get together and make a suggestion, and then we will also consult with the Prosecutor, or you can consult with the Prosecutor, and then we could reschedule these witnesses and decide who is going to be called when. In any case, those three witnesses can't come on the 26th because there will be no hearing. We will see whether you can make some suggestions after consulting with the Prosecutor. Thank you. Would you bring in the next witness. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Alilovic? Yes. Good day, Mr. Alilovic.

utterances.speaker: NIKO SAKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Alilovic. First of all I would like you to introduce yourself to the Court, to tell us your full name, your father's name, date of birth, and your address. Shall I repeat the question? Or have you heard it?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I heard it, but this doesn't fit well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We shall continue after you adjust it. Is it all right now?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Will you now answer my first question, and my first question refers to your general data so that the Court knows who you are.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Jozo Alilovic. I was born on the 27th of October, 1927, in the village of Nadioci in the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your address now?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: My address is the same because I still live where I was born.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the house have a number?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: It's number 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, what were your family circumstances? Who were you living with in your house in 1992 and 1993? I'm not referring to guests you may have had, but to the members of your household at that time.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: It was just my wife and me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many children did you have altogether?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Altogether I had six daughters, and they are all married, so none of them live with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your occupation now?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm retired now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I worked in the Zenica ironworks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: For 34 years. I worked for 34 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year did you retire in?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I retired in 1972 -- sorry; I mean '82. I apologise. '82. Five and three is eight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, how many living brothers and sisters did you have?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I had two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your brothers' names?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Marko and Tomislav.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old are they?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Marko is ten years younger than me. That means he was born in '37. And Tomislav was born in '52.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many sisters did you have?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Eight sisters? So eight sisters, two brothers, and you were the eleventh?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a bit hard to calculate how many of them there were altogether. When you retired, did you have a hobby you engaged in? For example, did you collect stamps, did you go hunting, fishing, gardening?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: When I retired, and before I retired, I was a hunter. I didn't go fishing. I went hunting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hunting game?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, hunting game, in the woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slowly. So as a hunter, were you a member of a hunting society?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I was a gamekeeper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you whether you were a member of a society.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the hunters' society, and I still am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of the society then of which you were a member?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: It was then called -- and I don't know if it's still called that, because everything has been interrupted -- but it was called Banovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you still a member?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I still am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a member of the hunting society and as hunter in 1992 and 1993, did you have the right to carry a hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1991, 1992, I was a gamekeeper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that mean, that you were a gamekeeper?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I was a gamekeeper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who appointed you to be a gamekeeper, and what were your tasks as a gamekeeper?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I was appointed by my organisation, my hunting society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was the administration that appointed you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the administration of the hunting society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your job as a gamekeeper?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: My job was, as a gamekeeper, whenever I could, to make a tour of the territory, whenever I was able to, to see whether, on the territory assigned to me, there was anyone hunting without permission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a gamekeeper, did you have a rifle?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I still do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not interested in now, but in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of rifle did you have?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I had a hunting rifle with two barrels. A shotgun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the big photograph to your right, can you show where your house was? You have to stand up, take the pointer, and the usher will help you a little. Could you stand to one side so that the Court can see what you are showing. Show us your house first, if you can find it. But take your time. Don't hurry, because this is upside down from the way we are used to looking at maps.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: My house is here. Both houses, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "both houses," did you have one house or several houses?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Two houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two houses. Did you build them both at the same time or at different times?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I built one 30 years ago, the one closer to the road, and I built the other one 10 years or 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that you have shown us your house, can you show us the houses of your neighbours and tell us the names of your neighbours? I don't mind what order you do it in, but please tell us whether each of these neighbours was a Muslim or a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: My closest neighbour was Redzep Elimanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he by nationality?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you tell us the name of each neighbour, please tell us what he was.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: My second neighbour was Muhamed Pezer, a Muslim. My third neighbour was my brother Tomislav. His house is here (indicating). Now, across the road is the house of my relative, Nikola Alilovic. Is that it? Here. Here, somewhere here (indicating), and then Mato Alilovic, Mirko's brother and my uncle, and my sister Kata. Probably around here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I think you have shown us enough neighbours, and you needn't go on. Please sit down. With reference to your Muslim neighbours, what were your relations with them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: With my Muslim neighbours? Until the first conflict, our relations were very good. After the first conflict, they were terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember when the first conflict occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: The first conflict occurred, I think, on the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how this change in the behaviour of Muslims toward you manifested itself?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I can't describe it exactly. I didn't avoid them. I didn't try to avoid them. I even helped them, as far as I was able, both during the first conflict and later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We shall talk about that later on. Can you tell us, your brother Tomislav, you showed us his house, and he was mentioned in these proceedings. Was he in his house, because you showed us his house, on the day the war broke out in 1993, on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to know is, when the war started, on the 16th of April, 1993, was your brother Tomislav in your village?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: My brother was in Germany, and he had arrived on the 15th of April, the day before the second conflict broke out, and he was staying with me. He was spending the night with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he came back from Germany the day before the conflict, and he was a guest in your house. We'll come back to that later. Can you tell us, since when is your brother in Germany?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he left 20 or 22 years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he has been working in Germany all this time?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is still working in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interested in the political events taking place in your municipality -- that is, the Vitez municipality -- since the first free elections?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm an elderly man. There are young people, and they should deal with politics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you lived as an old-age pensioner, and you went hunting?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have now arrived at the spring of 1992. Do you know anything about a former JNA barracks in Slimena?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I heard about it. I didn't go there. I was never there. But I heard there was a barracks. And my neighbour, Muhamed Pezer, went there by car, with a FAP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of car is that, when you say "FAP"?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a truck. It's a big truck, and he went there in early May, 1992, the 3rd or the 5th of May. He loaded the truck with metal, with iron --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I'm referring to weapons.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, weapons are a kind of metal. So he brought it home and distributed in his village of Ahmici to the men, anyone who was over ten years old, so that I saw young boys who were tending sheep and carrying these weapons, and they shot at anything that moved, even at birds, and I came to the conclusion that I had to tell my superiors in the hunting society that I was afraid to move around the territory I was supposed to guard or patrol, and I didn't go out any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were afraid of armed people?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because they were children, shooting at anything that moved, shooting at birds. Then I told my superiors that I could no longer perform my duty as a gamekeeper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muhamed Pezer who brought these weapons to the village, do you know anything about his political activity? What kind of person was he?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know because I was retired, and I only took an interest in my own life, and I couldn't know what activities he engaged in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Pezer Muhamed a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim, and he had a truck which he rented out for transport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the woods to see if there were any poachers there, did you have any unpleasant encounters which made you stop going to the woods?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With whom?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date. It was June. I was walking through the wood of Ivo Alilovic, Stipo's brother, and Mato Alilovic, and a man whose surname was Ahmic, but what was his name? Dear God, what's the name of that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fikret?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Fikret, yes, Fajkan's son, Fikret, that's right. He came out not far from his house, about 300 metres in front of me. He was armed. He had an automatic rifle, and he threatened me. He said I should never turn up again because if he saw me again at that place he would kill me and that I must never pass by that way again. So I apologised. I had to obey him because I saw that he was very tense, so I went home, and that was the last time I went out there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fikret Ahmic, is he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he had any position?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any special reason to threaten you? Were you in any kind of quarrel or dispute with him? Why would he tell you you were not allowed to go into the woods again?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I never had any kind of conflict with his father. We were good friends, and as regards Fikret himself and his brother Nusret, who is younger than him, I was always on good terms with them, and we never had any bad experiences, and that was the first time I had an unpleasant experience with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you ask him, "Fikret, what's the matter? Why shouldn't I go and see if there are any poachers in the woods? "

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was too afraid to ask him, so I didn't ask him anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take his threat seriously?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I took it seriously. He threatened me very seriously because he was pointing his automatic rifle at me, and he said if he ever saw me again he would kill me. That's how he threatened me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he pointed his automatic rifle, did he point it at you? Did he pull the trigger?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, he pointed it at me. That's all he did. He just pointed it at me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person called --

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm allowed to say the name, so I would like to ask the sound to be turned off. May we have a break now, since it's time for a break, and then we can start in a closed session after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to go to private session for a moment, please. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a good friend of yours, you said. Could you please tell us whether you had any conversations with him that you remember in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: From the time we were children, that person was a friend of mine and is a friend still. In June of 1992, I met with that person. He called me to go out to a cafe to have a coffee or maybe a few cognacs. We stayed there for awhile. I told that person that Mr. Fikret turned me back, like I explained earlier. That person asked me why had I been turned back. He did this because, above the village of Ahmici, there is a hill that is called Barin Gaj or Kruske (phoen), and he said, "Up there on that hill, there are 30 Mujahedeen." I don't know if I pronounced that properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the correct pronunciation is "Mujahedeen."

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these were not Mujahedeen. They were people from Krajina, Muslims who had escaped from the Krajina area and who were staying there. The village fed those people. The village objected; they said it was difficult for the village to feed them. So then they made an agreement, and that person said that those people should be transferred to the village of Lupac. The village of Lupac is not far. "If necessary and when necessary, they can easily come back." Hazim Ahmic did not permit for them to be transferred to Lupac. He took 20 and gave 10 of them to his brother, Esad. This is what that person told me in the cafe. We spent maybe two hours together in June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he perhaps say whether -- we won't call them "Mujahedeen"; we will call them Krajisniks (phoen). Were they armed or not?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No. He didn't say whether they were armed or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he didn't say whether they were armed or not, only just that so many people from Krajina had come?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, he didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village of Lupac, is that a Muslim or a Croat village?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: It's a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Hazim Ahmic; who is that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he's a Muslim. Is that the Hazim Ahmic who had a mosque? We talked about him.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he had a mosque in the village of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the month of September of that same year, did you see anything that would be out of the ordinary, as far as everyday living was concerned?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: September, that's the ninth month; right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In September, did you have any kind of incident with Fikret Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember what happened in the ninth month. I don't remember exactly. The cemetery that I saw on the photograph, I have a field of 10 dulum, and we were mowing the grass in September, six of us. Should I say who was there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Name them.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Ilija Lukic, myself, Franjo Maric, Anto Ninic -- Anto Ninic, I've said that -- Franjo Dujic, and Nikola Alilovic. We had finished mowing the grass early, maybe we had already finished by 4.00 or 4.30 in the afternoon, and we were going towards my house. We were passing below the cemetery to go out on the main road to go to my house. Across from the cemetery in the field, people were digging in several places. They were digging something. We came out on the road and we stopped, all six of us, and we asked the closest person that was there, what were they doing. They just simply answered that they were digging in order to bring in water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know the people who were digging?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we knew some of them, and the others, we did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which ones did you know, if you remember now?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember that we continued to stand there on the road and watch. Fikret Ahmic came up to us. He was carrying an automatic rifle on his back, and he either had a shovel or a pickaxe, and he said, "What are you looking at," could we just continue on our way? We should just go on where we were going. We just shrugged our shoulders, all six of us, and we went down the road to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't ask him why you had to go?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, we were afraid to ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among those people who were digging, did you recognise any of those people? You said that you did. Could you tell us the names?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were all our neighbours, but there were also some unfamiliar persons. From Ahmici, Nusret was there, his brother. I recognised him. I recognised several young and older people. They were all from Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there were several people that you didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did these people that you didn't know come from?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. I don't know where they were from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From September until the first conflict, which occurred on the 20th of October in '92, did anything happen that you would remember, anything unusual? Well, I see that you can't remember, so probably nothing did happen. Let's move on to the first conflict now, the conflict that happened on the 20th of October, '92. Could you tell the Court what you remember about that conflict?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of October, I was at my brother Tomo's house. Ilija Jukic and myself, that's my brother-in-law, my sister's husband, we were working on something up there on the 15th. At about 2.00 p.m. or maybe 3.00 p.m., not far from my brother Toma's house, maybe 30 or 40 metres away, people started to gather. They were beginning to dig, work on something, and they were bringing in different objects. They brought in a tripod, a metal tripod that is placed in front of tanks, and they placed it maybe 30 metres away from my house, next to the stream. They also brought in a large tank mine, and they had placed it on the road. I told my brother-in-law, "Let's move away from here because it's not good for us to be here." So we went back, not taking the road but going through the fields, back to my house. You couldn't hear anything. We didn't know anything. I didn't know anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about the day before, the 19th?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of those people who were placing the anti-tank mines?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were all of my neighbours. Muhamed Pezer was there and Fikret was there --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You don't need to name all of them.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: They were all of my neighbours. There were more of them. They would come and go. Some of them were putting up roadblocks; the others were digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next day.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: That evening, I didn't hear or see anybody passing, even though the main road passes about eight metres away from my front door. I didn't see anybody or hear anybody the whole night. Nobody moved anywhere. In the morning, I was interested in going out to see what was going on. Somewhere, in some places, I could see the occasional soldier in a uniform, but I didn't get close because I didn't know who they were. At about 9.00 a.m., maybe before that, maybe at 8.30, I'm not sure, a shot was heard close to Muhamed Pezer's house. I heard one or two shots. I turned around, and I could see Muhamed Pezer coming out of his house. He was carrying a rifle in his hands, and they shot him and wounded him in the leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw this?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw this. He threw the rifle away in the middle of his field. He ran to the road because he was halfway between the road and his house, maybe 20 -- there's 20 or 50 metres from his house to the road, so he was halfway. He ran across the street into my field, and then through my field, he ran away and ran in the direction of my cousin Mato's house. After about half an hour, I wanted to see what had happened to him, so I went to my cousin Mato's house. I found in my cousin Mato's house Elvid Sacir and his wife, they are both Muslim; Pero Alilovic and his wife, these are Croats; Mato Alilovic and his wife, they're Croats. Then Ivo Alilovic and Mato's brother's wife, they were all sitting there on the floor. Muhamed Pezer was lying on the couch. They had wrapped his leg in something. Mato's wife was sitting on the floor and wiping his forehead with a towel. Mato offered me a brandy to drink, and I didn't want to. I was standing there for about ten minutes, and then I went home. When I went home, I started to go behind his house, to go through the woods, but the earth started to shatter in front of me. I could hear gunfire, and I got scared, so I went back to Mato's house. They all asked me, "What's the matter with you?" "Nothing is the matter with me," but they said, "You've turned white," and I said, "Well, I can't see. I don't know." So then I told him to give me a brandy. Mato gave me a brandy, a glass of brandy, and then I said, "Please, can I have another one?" So he actually poured me two. I stayed in Mato's house for ten minutes. Then I went out on the road, and then I went on the other side, behind Mato's house to my house. I got to my house. I didn't go inside. A car arrived up to my house, and I was called, "How can I go to the house of Nesib Kajmakovic? He's a Muslim." I answered, "Friend, in no case can you go to their house because there is fighting. There is fighting from here and from here," and he was supposed to go through the middle. So I said, "Friend, there is no way you can go to the Kajmakovic house. Nesib Kajmakovic has been wounded." He was supposed to go to take him. Then I told him, "There is a wounded man in Mato's house. Take him." Then he said, "Take me there so I can see where it is." I went to the same road. I went in front of the car. He went behind me in the car up to Mato's house, and I told Mato at the door, "Take him into the car." So he brought -- so Sacir, Elvid, Pero and Mato, I don't know if there was anybody else, they took him out to the car and sent him to the hospital in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he seriously wounded or was that just a scratch?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I only saw that he was wrapped. I couldn't see the wound, but he couldn't come out of Mato's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the shooting start?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly when the shooting started. I don't know how long it went on for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The wounded man that you talked about and whom you helped to get to a medical aid, was he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim, Muhamed Pezer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now go to the day before the war started, so that's the 15th of April, 1993. Could you please tell the Court what you did that day, so the day before the war started?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I was at my brother Toma's house because he was in Germany, so I was hoping he would get there. I went up to his house to do some work there, to fence something off. My brother came --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he come?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: He came in the evening quite late. He took the bus to Vitez, and then he came up to his house. Then we went to my house to spend the night, and that evening, my brother Tomislav spent the night at my house, not at his house. On the 16th --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're still talking about the 15th. On the 15th, did you know what would happen the next day?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't know anything?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody knew anything. Nobody had any idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you right, on the 15th, the day was like any other day?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will now show what your house looks like, and then we will continue with the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Would the usher please assist?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D15/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alilovic, could you put this on the machine beside you? Could you show us on this photograph -- wait a minute. Just a moment, please. Could you describe photograph number 1? Could you tell us what photograph 1 shows?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Photograph number 1 shows my old house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Show us your old house with the pointer, please. We can't see.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The old house. Can you see the new house?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see the new house. This is it (indicating), but you can't see the door because it's behind the old house. This is the window. This is the veranda of the new house. This is the roof of the new house. This is my apple tree in front of my new house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe photograph number 2, please? This is number 2. Could you describe photograph number 2?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 2. They are numbered on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, number 2, this is the old house (indicating), and this is my new house right behind it. There's a passage here between the houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Both of the houses are inside the same yard; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe photograph number 3?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Photograph number 3 shows my old house. You can see the roof, the walls of the old house. You can see the woods there further on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can see part of the yard too; right?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see a good part of the yard, the snow here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since these photographs were taken much later, they were taken this year, obviously while there was still snow on the ground, from 1993 until the day these photographs were taken, did anything change?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing has changed, no. Everything is still the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When your brother arrived on the 15th and came to stay with you, did you stay in the old house or the new house?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: We slept in the old house. I still sleep in the old house, even today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is in the new house?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: There's no one. No one. I'm all alone. I can't sleep in two houses at once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us what happened on the first day of the war, the 16th of April? How did you wake up?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: My brother, my wife, and I were awakened by gunfire. I can't tell you exactly what time it was, but it was sometime around 6.30 perhaps. I'm not certain. There was gunfire, and we didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who was firing?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No. We knew nothing because neither my brother nor I had gone out at night, and we knew nothing and saw nothing. We were awakened by gunfire. We jumped up. My wife was the first to jump up, and she started running outside, but I stopped her and said, "Don't go out because we don't know what's going on," so she didn't go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the gunfire started, did you stay in the old house or did you move to the new one?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: We were in the old house that morning. We happened to be in the old house when the gunfire started. We hadn't moved to the new house. We were afraid to go out because we didn't know what was going on, so we didn't go to the new house. The gunfire started, as I said, so we peered out of the windows to see if we could see anything, to see if we could see what was going on. We saw smoke coming from the house of Pezer Ahmic. We saw it had been set on fire and was smoking. I said, "Tomislav, we should run and put out the fire, but how can we when they're shooting?" So we didn't go out. We didn't leave the old house all day. I don't the exact time, the hour, a car arrived --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't mention that name. We shall mention the name in the same way as we did the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Could we go into closed session for a moment because we are now arriving at a protected witness? (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Be careful. If you mention the name, you can be punished. So tell us what went on.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: They called me out, and one of the soldiers said to me, "Jozo. Keep this child with you until I come back."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Then I recognised the boy, and I told him to come in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know his parents, his family?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know his family very well. They are my neighbours. Yes, I know them very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go on with your story.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: The child entered my house. The child was dressed in pyjamas and was all wet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he frightened?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was terrified. He was all wet, so my wife undressed him. She took his underpants off, his pyjamas, and his slippers, and she gave him dry clothes because the child was shivering. The child was cold, shivering with cold and with fear. The child stayed with us for 13 days or 12 days, and then INFOR came, it was UNPROFOR, and they took him to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you let his mother know in any way that her son was with you?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Since the little boy didn't know where his parents were, since the boy said that his father and his elder brother had left or, rather, had gone to the mosque to a meeting and that his father had locked the door from the outside and taken the key with him, when some soldiers arrived at his house, nobody could open the door, either those outside or those inside, but they handed the boy and his elder brother and his elder sister out over the balcony, and his mother as well. The boy was told to go toward the road, and it was cold, wet. There was a lot of water. That's why he was wet when he arrived at my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you what happened to his family?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: He told me that his brother had been killed. I kept telling him, "No, no, they haven't done it," and he said, "Yes, I saw it. They wanted to kill me, too, but a soldier wouldn't let them." And he told me to run to the road, and then two other soldiers came by in a car and took him into their car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I asked if you had told his mother.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had a telephone, and I knew the number because he told he the telephone number in his home but no one answered. So we called acquaintances to find out where his mother was, and we found out that she was in Travnik. So when I let his mother know that the boy was with me, she dropped the telephone. I didn't know what was going on, but it was because she fainted. She fell to the ground and dropped the telephone. Later they told me that everything was all right, and then I said that she shouldn't worry about anything because I would look after the child to the best of my ability and that the child would want for nothing, and that's how it was until they took him from me, and when he left me he was well and he was healthy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of vehicle did UNPROFOR use to pick up the boy?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they came with two small packages of food, and I don't know what happened afterwards because none of them contacted me later on to tell me how he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to the 16th of April. When this boy came, did you put him in the old house or the new house?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: When he arrived, perhaps it was about 9.00 in the morning, or half past nine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the first day, the 16th?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, the 16th? The 16th, yes. He came into the room in the old house, and he followed me everywhere. Then we moved from the old house because it wasn't so stable. There were no concrete slabs, and there are two in the new house, so because of the shelling, we moved to new house, the boy and my wife, and my brother while he was staying with me, and I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day when the war started, were you afraid that your brother Tomislav might be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't easy, because they would come to my house -- first three soldiers came, but they didn't say anything to Tomislav. They didn't tell him that he should go with them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But weren't you afraid of this possibility?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were. We were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when these soldiers came to your door, did you put your brother Tomislav in the other house with the boy? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: That whole day, the boy and Tomislav and I were in the old house, that whole day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were all together?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the boy was in the house, too, when three soldiers came?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the three soldiers came, the boy was in the kitchen in the old house with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time did the soldiers come?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: On that day the soldiers came at perhaps about -- hmm -- about 12.00, it might have been. I'm not certain, but about 12.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what they looked like? Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all three of them were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: One of them was wearing a black uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm asking you about the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was some kind of rifles?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Some kind of rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: One was wearing black, and the other two were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any kind of insignia?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: They had HVO insignia, as far as I was able to see and understand. They had HVO insignia on their sleeves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You noticed nothing else?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was a long time ago, and I didn't think of paying attention to their insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know these young men who arrived?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know them, but if I may say, they came to my yard and asked me if I had a telephone. I said I did. So all three of them entered the house. One of them rang up his father and mother, and another one rang up his girlfriend. My wife was outside, and then a fourth soldier came in on his own, into my yard, and my wife called to me to come out, and a young man in uniform with weapons arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: A military uniform. A camouflage uniform. HVO. He had the same kind of insignia as the first three. He came to the yard, and he was weeping. He was the neighbour of my wife's family from her native village. She's from Busovaca, from Dusina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of that young man?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: His father is Jure Kegelj, but I don't know his name. This young man said, since he knew my wife, he said, "Old woman, you're not asking me why I am crying." So she said, "What's the matter, son? Are you wounded?" He said "No." So she said, "And what's the matter?" And he said, "I have no family left. They have all been killed and massacred." He was asking for some water to wash his face, and he went on weeping. So my old woman asked me to come out of the house, and I did, and the third soldier rang up someone, but I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about the one who came to the yard on his own.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: So I went out. I didn't know this young man, but I knew his father, because I had gone to parties with his father when we were young men. We are of the same generation, and we were fellow workers, so I knew his family, but I didn't know the children. I didn't know the young man, but my wife told me whose child he was. So I asked him, "Are you Jure's son?" And he said "Yes." So he came in, and he just stood there like a statue. He wouldn't sit down. I offered him a glass of brandy, but he refused, and then that young boy was in the house with us. When he was in the house he didn't say anything. All four of them, all four soldiers went out and left down the road to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The boy you said was from Dusina, is that the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: It's the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the younger soldier who arrived last was from Dusina; what about the first three? Could you conclude where they might be from?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the two who used the telephone, who talked on the telephone, I gathered that both of them were from Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what basis did you conclude this?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from what they said when they were talking to the people they rang up. They were asking about certain places, so they were ringing up their families. One of them called his father and mother, and the other one called his girlfriend. So I concluded that they were from around Kiseljak. I don't know about the third one because I didn't hear him talking on the telephone because I was outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you what army unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you what they'd been doing that morning?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't say anything at all. I didn't dare ask them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do. They're my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know them well?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Quite well?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, the first day of the war, did they come to your house?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you certain?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the young man who was in your house couldn't have seen them?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No one could have seen them. I didn't see them. And the boy who was at my house, he never went out that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether you know Sakib Ahmic, son of Rasid?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, that's also my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the Muslims ever thank you about this boy and about that wounded person that you mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sakib Ahmic, did he stop by a couple of months ago?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, maybe one and a half months ago, he came by. Zijo Kajmakovic came by. Zijo Kajmakovic has a house in the village in the direction of my house, so he came along with Sakib Ahmic. They stopped by my house, on the road, they just stopped in the ditch, and I came out to the road to them. Sakib Ahmic was in the car, and Zijo Kajmakovic. We were talking about everything, and I told Sakib, and he asked me whether the boy was at my house, and I said, "Yes, but unfortunately his mother or his father still haven't contacted me." Then he thanked me. He said, "Aferim to you for doing what you did. We heard what had happened, so bless you and thank you from me."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what kind of a man was Sakib Ahmic? Can you tell us something about him?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I know him as a driver. He was mostly driving around in Vitez, some officials there. I don't know whether this was a company, Impregnacija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: He was very -- he was in very good relations with me. There was no revenge. He never said a bad thing to me, nor did I say anything bad to him, but I don't know what he was like towards others, but I know that he was a bit sharp. He liked to kind of quarrel everywhere, to interfere. That's the only thing that I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Zoran and Mirjan? Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what to say about Zoran or Mirjan. Very few people knew about those boys. They never bothered anybody. If there was some kind of jolly company, that's where they would be. But if they were somewhere else, then I wouldn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I only would like for the photographs to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. No objection, I assume? It is admitted into evidence. Counsel Pavkovic, are any Defence counsel ready to cross-examine this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Alilovic. My name is Franck Terrier. I'm one of the Prosecution attorneys. I'm going to ask you a few questions following your testimony. I would like to know whether at that time in Ahmici somebody else had the same name -- that is, the same first and last name -- as yourself.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking that question because at least two witnesses who came to testify at this Tribunal stated that Jozo Alilovic was seen keeping guard in 1993 on the Radak Bridge, and in light of what you've said, I was asking whether that was the same person or whether there was another person who has the same name.

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody could have seen me anywhere on that day other than in my yard and in my house because I didn't move anywhere on that day. And not only on that day, but maybe for several days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know anybody named Jozo Alilovic, another person who has the name Jozo Alilovic?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: I do, but in Vitez. He's a cousin of mine. Jozo Alilovic, called Bego. That's my relative, but he's in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old is he? Can you tell us what year he was born?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe he is two or three years younger than I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does he have any children?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Boys, girls?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: He has sons and daughters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Alilovic, let's speak for a few moments about your experience as a hunter. You told us that for a long time you had been a hunter, that you liked hunting, that in 1991 and 1992 you were a gamekeeper. What kind of game would you catch in the woods around Ahmici, Santici, and Pirici? What kind of game did you hunt?

utterances.speaker: JOZO ALILOVIC
utterances.text: You could hunt only those animals that were allowed, permitted, by the hunting society in the season. When it was rabbit-hunting season, then rabbit.
